name: Notification destinations
summary: send the notifications you pick to places outside the app, with one routing matrix that says which notification goes where.
description: Twelve kinds of destination, many instances of each: slack, discord, microsoft teams (workflows webhook), telegram, ntfy, pushover, a generic signed webhook, email (smtp), sms through aws sns, sms through twilio, pagerduty, and every web push device. Every secret, recipient and number lives in the Keychain and is write-only. One matrix lists 29 notification types in families (needs you, sessions, accounts, health, app, in-app only) against a screen column plus one column per destination. Every cell can be unticked, needs-you included; needs-you starts ticked. Hiding a card hides the pop-up only: the bell, the history, the status light and the tray keep everything. Each destination can add away mode, quiet hours, a reminder and a project filter, and can opt in to details (tool and target, or the question snippet; scrubbed, capped at 200 characters, never on sms). The message carries a link back, tried in order: the mobile sync public address, then the local name, then the network address, then no link. A pause switch holds all outside delivery on one computer. Settings and secrets sync to paired computers over the paired link, secrets landing in each computer's Keychain; any tick or destination can be pinned to one computer. An agent can send you a notification with the notify tool. The old Slack, ntfy and Pushover secrets move into the Keychain.
where: Settings, notifications tab, destinations: add, test, edit and delete each destination.
Settings, notifications tab, routing: the matrix, the link back, and the pause switch.
Settings, notifications tab, alerts on this device: each web push device appears as its own column in the matrix.
how_to: Open settings, notifications, destinations, press add a destination, pick a kind from the grouped list (each service has its logo; click the field or use the arrow keys, type to filter), fill in its fields and press add. Secrets are write-only: once saved they show as set, and a blank field keeps the stored one. A webhook generates a signing secret for you and shows it once.
Press test on a destination to send one fixed test message; one test every 10 seconds.

Open settings, notifications, routing. Tick a notification under a destination to send it there. The screen column decides which cards pop up; needs-you rows start ticked and can be unticked like any other. A tick on the new destination column sets what a new destination starts with.
Turn on this computer only, then change a tick: it is pinned here with a local badge and does not sync. Press reset to global on a pinned cell to go back to the synced value.

On a destination, set away mode (hold a notification while you are active at this computer, and send it once you are away), quiet hours (needs-you notifications still go through), a reminder (minutes, or off) and a project filter (empty means all projects). Turn on details to add the tool and target or the question snippet; sms never gets details.

Under routing, read the link line: it says which link outside messages carry (mobile sync address, local name, network address or none) and why. Use the pause switch to hold all outside delivery on this computer.
With a paired computer, settings and secrets sync over the paired link, and each computer keeps secrets in its own Keychain. Pin an item to keep this computer's value.

An agent in a session can call the notify tool to send you one notification of type agent.message, routed by the matrix. The switch is mcp.agent_notify (PUT /api/v1/mcp-admin/agent-notify); off hides the tool.
Existing Slack, ntfy and Pushover settings move into Keychain-backed destinations on their own and the plaintext is removed from config.json and its backup.

A self-hosted webhook or ntfy server that only speaks http (n8n, Home Assistant) on your own network: on its form turn on allow private addresses, then allow plain http on this network, and use an http:// address. Both switches are for this computer only and never sync. While plain http is on, the message and any auth header cross your network unencrypted; only private addresses are allowed, and a public address stays refused.
examples: You walk away from your desk: the permission and question notifications go to your phone through ntfy or Pushover, and a quiet-hours window keeps the finished-turn pings off at night while a permission request still gets through.
A shared channel gets a Slack message when a session dies, but with details off, so no command or file name leaves the computer.
Your laptop and your desktop are paired: add a destination once and it appears on both, with its secret stored in each computer's Keychain.
A destination fails five times in a row with a permanent error: it is switched off and a notifications health alert tells you, without that alert being sent outside.

Home Assistant at http://homeassistant.local:8123 receives your session notifications through a webhook, with plain http turned on for this computer only; the same destination synced to your laptop sits quietly there with a note that plain http is off on that computer, and is never switched off for it.
